content_voiceover: This slide shows the pivotal New England Journal of Medicine paper behind dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab in PMBCL, the Dunleavy study that established this regimen as a chemotherapy-alone option, without consolidative mediastinal radiation. The four panels show event-free and overall survival separately for the NCI cohort and the Stanford validation cohort. Look at how flat and high these curves stay out to ten-plus years, there's an early drop in the first year or so in the NCI cohort, reflecting the handful of early treatment failures, but after that the curve barely moves, and the Stanford cohort curves are essentially flat from the start. The headline numbers on the right say it clearly, five-year progression-free survival of ninety-three percent and five-year overall survival of ninety-seven percent, achieved with chemotherapy alone. This is the evidence base for the practice you just learned, treat with dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab, restage with PET, and if the scan is clean, you can often avoid radiation entirely, sparing young patients, who are disproportionately young women, from the long-term cardiac and breast cancer risks of mediastinal radiotherapy.
keypoints: Landmark NEJM study establishing dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab for PMBCL without radiation
Curves stay flat after an early first-year drop, validated across NCI and Stanford cohorts
Rationale: avoiding radiation spares young, predominantly female patients from long-term cardiac and breast cancer risk
keypoint_voiceover: This is the trial to cite when you're asked why PMBCL can be treated without radiation. Dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab alone achieved five-year progression-free survival of ninety-three percent and overall survival of ninety-seven percent, validated in both the NCI and Stanford cohorts. That outcome is why a PET-negative scan after chemo supports skipping radiotherapy, which matters most because these patients are young and disproportionately female, exactly the population most vulnerable to radiation's late cardiac and breast cancer risks.
